title: Passover: leading a seder
hook: anyone can lead a seder with a simple Haggadah
tomorrow: can you add your own question to an old script?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cleaning: search where food goes, and the crumbs you miss become dust. Dust is not chametz. The kitchen is ready. Now somebody has to run the night.
screen: `DUST IS NOT CHAMETZ.` → `SOMEBODY HAS TO RUN THE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's an odd stage direction for a dinner party. The seder's script expects a child to ask why tonight is different. So the Talmud asks the obvious next question: what if there's no child at the table? Its answer gets stranger as it goes. Then a spouse asks. If there's no spouse, you ask yourself. And two scholars who already know every answer still ask each other. A person alone at a table, asking out loud why this night is different. Why would a script keep going when nobody's there to ask?
screen: `AN ODD STAGE DIRECTION.` → `NO CHILD? A SPOUSE ASKS.` → `ALONE? ASK YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: The Torah gives the job in one line: "And thou shalt tell thy son in that day, saying: It is because of that which the LORD did for me when I came forth out of Egypt." The book that runs the night is the Haggadah, from the Hebrew for telling. It's a script with stage directions: bless the wine, wash hands, dip a green vegetable, break the matzah, ask, tell, eat, sing. The Mishnah adds that if the child doesn't know how to ask, the parent teaches them. Now the puzzle solved. The Talmud, in Pesachim, follows the question all the way down, from a child to a spouse to yourself to two scholars, because the seder isn't a test of whether the leader knows enough. It's a promise that the story gets told out loud, by whoever is there. That's why anyone can lead one. A simple Haggadah, a few people, the questions read in English, a short telling, the meal. Some seders run late into the night with commentary. Some are short, with a toddler under the table. Both are seders. The leader's real job is small and doable: keep the questions coming, and make sure the story gets said.
screen: `THOU SHALT TELL THY SON.` · `HAGGADAH: THE TELLING.` · `A CHILD, A SPOUSE, YOURSELF.` · `KEEP THE QUESTIONS COMING.` · then, large: `YOU CAN LEAD IT.`

segments.voice: Take a scrap of paper and write three short lines: what you'll bless, what you'll ask, what you'll eat. That's the bones of a short seder: the wine and its blessing, the questions and the story, then the meal. Read your three lines back once, slowly, and notice that the whole night fits on one small page.
Passover: the festival of the exodus, and its seder, a night run by a script made of questions, the Haggadah.
Hold on to this one: you can lead it, with a simple Haggadah and whoever shows up. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: At a Passover seder, one person usually leads from a Haggadah while everyone reads parts; seders range from long nights of commentary to short ones built around young children.
